sources.citation: Pittayaporn, Pittayawat. 2009. The phonology of Proto-Tai. PhD dissertation, Cornell University, Ithaca. xix+417 pp. (Sapa = dialect no. 48 in the 68-dialect sample; data from the author's unpublished fieldnote 'Tay of Sapa' (Pittayaporn 2007e), fieldwork winter 2008.)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing about stress in Sapa. Sapa appears only as a comparative data point: p. 20 (fieldwork on 'the Tai dialects of Sapa, Bao Yen, and Cao Bang'), p. 302 ('This variety is extremely similar to subgroup Q [= SWT], but did not go through the change from *kr- to *ʰr-'), p. 309, p. 319 (dialect list, source 'Pittayaporn (2007e)'), plus the lexical appendix. The only stress discussion is the general foot typology (Hayes 1995) and sesquisyllabic-vs-monosyllabic prosodic-word argument for Proto-Tai (ch. 2), not a statement about Sapa.

sources.citation: Edmondson, Jerold A., Kenneth J. Gregerson & Nguyễn Văn Lợi. n.d. (c. 1998-2000). Padi [pa31 zi31] and F. Tay Sa Pa'.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing on stress. Says Padi is 'in terms of tone splits, tone values, phonology, and lexicon coincidentally very similar to Central Thai of Bangkok City'; 'We also examined Tay Sa Pa of Lao Cai. It has been similarly grouped in Tay, even though it too is, in fact, a SW Tai language. There are about 300 speakers each of Padi and Tay Sa Pa.' Lettered sites (incl. F Tay Sa Pa, 1995-97) have sound files 'on CD-ROM only'.
